newsitem.title: USA: Experienced partner a plus in starting a business.
newsitem.headline: Experienced partner a plus in starting a business.

text.p: When Janden and Bill Richards decided to leave their corporate jobs for the challenge of their own business, they relied on an experienced partner to get them started.
Their story is a lesson in the advantage of linking up with someone who knows a lot more than you do, and the importance of trust in a business partnership.

In the summer of 1994, the Richards bought a half-interest in Zimmerman Foods Inc., a Lancaster, Pa., company that makes relishes, preserves, cup cheese and other handmade food spreads in the fashion of Lancaster County's Amish community.

The company markets its products through wholesalers and manufacturers' representatives under the Shenk's Handmade in the Heart of Amish Country label. Its small retail stand in downtown Lancaster's central market, the oldest indoor farmers' market in the country, has been a landmark since the turn of the century.

The Richards' long-time friend, Bill Zimmerman, bought the company from the founding Shenk family nine years ago. After running it on his own, Zimmerman came to the conclusion that he was unable to give it enough attention, and asked the Richards to join him as partners.

At the time, Janden Richards was working as director of art and design development at the Binney & Smith unit of Hallmark Cards in Easton, Pa. She drove 90 minutes each way from the couple's home in Philadelphia, and her husband, who spent most of his career in the office furniture industry, ran a factory for a medium-sized metal-working operation.

"I was perfectly happy in manufacturing," said Bill Richards. "We loved living in Philadelphia, and one day we were having lunch with Bill and his wife Patty, and they asked if we'd like to come in with them.

"Who wouldn't give up a couple of 6-figure incomes and life in the big city for the possibility of no income and life in rural America for the opportunity of working for yourself?" he said facetiously. "It seemed like a good idea."
They had the company appraised and paid Zimmerman for 50 percent of the stock. Although a formal partnership agreement was drawn up, it was never finalised.
The Richards say they would not have considered leaving their jobs had they not had such strong trust in their friend and faith in his mentoring.

"We wouldn't have got into it without him. We didn't have enough knowledge of what was needed," said Bill Richards. "I was confident in his ability to help us get through this thing. Working with him and talking with him, and knowing what he was adding to the situation was what got us into it."

Zimmerman, who had worked for an international mining company before setting up his own speciality metals company, said he had no doubt about teaching the Richards what was needed to run the business. But he was concerned about their making the transition from the corporate environment.

"I discovered I had to change my mentality signficantly, and it took me some time to do that when I left my employer," he said. "The kind of reality that sets in when you are working for your next paycheck -- and it's totally up to you to make that occur -- is something that I think very few people are prepared for coming from a corporate type of environment.
"My only doubts were whether they really had the ability to make that transition, and how long it would take them to do that."

Janden Richards had helped Zimmerman design packaging for Shenk's products, but realised that even with her managerial experience and her husband's production background, the two did not possess the needed financial and marketing skills.

"I didn't have a very strong financial background, and I definitely needed to partner with someone who could take the lead in that area, as opposed to thinking I could do everything myself," she said. "You can't. Everyone has strengths and weaknesses.

"If we were going to just start our own business, I don't think we would have had all of the collective skills we would have needed," she added. "Partnering with someone who already was doing a business for himself for 15 years helped the learning process."
Their training was more informal than formal, and for the first year, the couple did every job in the company, which has only one other full-time and two part-time employees.

"We cooked, we spent time with customers, we did the books," said Janden Richards. "It all needed to be done, and it gave us a feel for the business. My husband cooked for about a year. He knows how to cook everything now."

Corporate strategy was also informal. "From time to time we would have weekly meetings and strategise and decide what had to be done and when," she said. "We just agreed who would take care of what and went out and did it."

The company has revenues of about $500,000 annually, about the same as when the Richards came in. But they are now ready to take it to the next stage, and have targeted specific products and areas for growth.

At the same time, they are also preparing to buy the company's building and real estate and plan eventually to buy Zimmerman's share of the business. That was part of the original plan, the Richards said.

"You really have to know up front what the end result is going to be," said Bill Richards. "If you're going to partner with somebody and they plan on continuing being a partner, that's one thing. But if they plan on divesting themselves, it's different.
"We knew Bill would eventually leave us on our own, and it's been a crash course in the business," he said.
Although the Richards say they had no misgivings about their lack of a formal agreement with their partner, they admit such an arrangement is potentially dangerous.
"That's something you couldn't do if you didn't have the kind of relationship that we have," said Bill Richards. "That's something I wouldn't recommend anyone doing."
